utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honour. Case number IT-03-67-PT, The Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today is the 20th of August, 2007. My greetings to all the people in the courtroom. Ms. Dahl and your associates, my greetings to Mr. Seselj, and to all the people in the courtroom. As you know, this Status Conference is the follow-up of the conference we finished at ten past 7.00 last Friday. We are continuing with our work, and in order to do so I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Seselj, because he couldn't quite finish what he had to say last time. I had to interrupt him because it was getting late. You have the floor, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, last Friday I started speaking about the relevance of the material disclosed to me by the OTP. The OTP so far has disclosed up to 1.000 documents out of a total of 4.000, and they have serving documents on me in other ways, documents like requests to take note of some evidence. Many of them are not relevant at all, and they are just an unnecessary burden that is making normal work more difficult for me. And if they continue serving irrelevant documents on me, the cell next door to mine will not be enough storage, I will have will have to spread to the entire floor. Let me illustrate this to you, judge. I brought three binders, and if you would be so kind just to ask the usher to take them, and just take a look for a second I will explain these three binders. They served me complete photocopies of church books from Hrtkovci in Vojvodina, the registries of births, deaths, marriages, baptisms from 1945 to 2000. It's absolutely irrelevant, we have statistics on the population of Hrtkovci. We know the present and the past population by name. It's a small village of several thousand inhabits in the municipality of Ruma so that was absolutely unnecessary. This is just an illustration of how they work. You will also see a copy of the 1974 constitution of the SFRY which I have in three copies. Then the book of Borislov Jovic, The Last Days of SFRY, 400 pages they served on me three times. They served on me three times, once there 2006, and now in two copies. Now what happened, in one package, in one box which fits four -- five binders, one binder contains the entire photo copy of the Borislov Jovic's book, another binder is another copy of Borislav Jovic's book. It was done by different people, and they just filled the box randomly without mutual coordination and that's how they served it on me. I know the OTP has gotten used to working that way in many other cases. They are also used to most other Defence counsel not reading this, not researching, but now they've run into someone who at least leafs through and now they have a problem. Last time I said, if you remember, that I would insist, in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Evidences, that the Office of the Prosecutor gives an explanation for each document in particular, why that document is relevant, to provide the grounds. They are obliged to do so under the rules. In many cases they have not done so because the Defence did not require it. The lawyer would just look, glance, say to himself it doesn't really concern his client and he would let go. Court evidence must contain exclusively relevant documents and trials can only be based on relevant documents. Trials don't take place here really in that way, although maybe be there is an exception I have not run across, but this is just an illustration. The list would be very long indeed if I gave you all the examples. There is the founding document of Jovan Raskovic's party, and then the socialist party of Bosnia and Herzegovina, photocopies of all kinds of legislation in multiple copies, the same text in multiple copies. The same text. Textbooks of the Military Academy, on the Command Staff Academy, and the so-called General's School, the school of warfare. The Office of the Prosecutor continues to serve me documents in English. I returned already two large bundles of such documents, and in their latest letter they informed me that they would serve me both in English and in B/C/S because there is special indexation, special numbering in English, and I might need it. I will never need anything in English. If documents in B/C/S do not have certain numbers, then it is their problem. They will have to identify the document for me in Serbian, because I'm not really interested in what's written in English. But sometimes they give me a document solely in English, because they probably don't expect me to look at it. I received a couple of such documents in the past few days, and I underlined those that were only in English. Sometimes there would be complete binders about Islamic culture. Islamic monuments involving Bosnia-Herzegovina, et cetera. They all -- they have to translate it all for me into Serbian. Some of them are 1.000 pages long. They thought it would just pass through among the multitude of other documents. I will let nothing pass. Further more, I've already said that the documents that are potentially exculpatory, they failed to disclose at all for the most part. I received sometimes something sporadically. It's a negligible number compared to 2.700 pages that they have admitted exist, and they promised to disclose them to me. Then again I am facing the problem of the OTP's request to admit into evidence certain documents accompanied by earlier statements and testimony of witnesses who are dead. There are five such witnesses, who are no longer alive in my case, out of which at least three testified in earlier cases. Some continue to be protected although they are dead because the OTP insists on it and that's why I'm not going to mention any names. I'm not going to mention any names of either protected or unprotected witnesses. First of all I'm going to oppose any admission into evidence of witness statements of those who are dead, especially the statement of Milan Babic by virtue of his suicide during his testimony Martic case, Babic denied everything that he has said, in a way that could not be more eloquent. There is no surer way of proving that what all he said on the orders of the Prosecution is a pure lie. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (redacted). Another also committed suicide. He continues to be protected here. He was convicted, he served his sentence, he returned home, and committed suicide. The Office of the Prosecutor did not give me at all the testimony of the transcripts of Milan Babic in the Martic case in other cases. Babic testified in Milosevic, and Krajisnik and partially in the Martic case. The Prosecution informs me they had filed a request to admit those transcripts into evidence. They gave me some of the documents that were admitted into evidence through Babic, but there is no material of his testimony. I found the plea bargain, the agreed facts to exist, but none of those documents I received. So I cannot state my position, whether I agreed to their admission or not, until I receive the complete documentation. I informed you in one of my submissions that I will oppose it, but on the other hand I cannot definitively say that I am going to oppose it until I receive them. When will I receive them? It's high time now. Are they intending to serve me with 200.000 documents five days before the trial? Now is the time if the trial is going to begin in November. I'm ready for a trial in November. Even if they let me have everything a month before the trial, that's enough. That's enough notice. Even if is 4.000.000 documents, I'll read them. But I know what will happen here because that has happened in other cases. They will disclose a part, but they won't disclose the greatest part. They will disclose it successively and belatedly. What about the material the Prosecution was aware of back in 2003 that is exculpatory. What use will it be to me if it's served once the trial is over? What purpose does it serve they then? It has to be disclosed before the trial. I have to ask you, Judge, to make it incumbent upon the OTP to disclose all the relevant documents under 66 and under 68 a month before the trial at the latest. And to make it clear to them that after the beginning of the trial, they are not allowed to serve on me any document, not a single document they were aware of before the beginning of the trial and failed to serve. I don't know rule out the possibility that they may later get hold of another, of a new relevant document. That happens in trials. Something new is learned, something new is found and that can be disclosed to me during the trial. But they cannot disclose to me during the trial things they are have in their possession and were aware of before the trial. Then I will be a victim of that trial. How am I supposed to defend myself? I've already said that I am completely in agreement for the trial to begin in November. I'm really looking forward to it and I am impatient, but some things have to be made clear before that. The Prosecution has many more protected witnesses than unprotected witnesses. They have to disclose those names to me at least a month before the trial begins, not before the witness appears to testify. Every decision that has been made so far concerning protective measures contain the clause stipulating that the name of the protected witness must be disclosed to me a month before the trial. A month. Last year they tried to begin the trial without this disclosure. They disclosed five or six names to me 15 days before the beginning of the trial but not the rest of the names and the Trial Chamber tolerated that. I think that you, Judge, and your colleagues who will be dealing with this case will not tolerate that, because otherwise I will have to resort to other measures of non-institutional struggle. I insist on my rights, if my rights are brutally violated, then I have to resort to fighting this in other ways. There was discussion last time on the way the Prosecution will lead its evidence. The Prosecution itself admitted recently in one of its documents that they would, in a large measure, introduce their evidence through written statements. I oppose that. Witnesses have to testify viva voce. Rules -- Rule 92 bis, ter, and quater derive from 89 (F), apply only in exceptional cases. It says there in the text "in the interest of justice," their interest of justice has to be proven first. In every specific case, it has to be proven that it is indeed in the interest of justice that the statement of a witness should be admitted into evidence without direct examination, without actually doing it lightly. It has been done before, but this is not a positive legal practice that should be followed. It is a very grave deformation of the legal process. I dealt with it in great detail. What if, for instance, your Trial Chamber decides to admit this, and I am very close to thinking, although I haven't decided yet, that in that case, it's maybe better for me to give up on cross-examination. If there is no direct examination then why would I cross-examine? Why would I cross-examine a zombie witness. A witness who is not even capable of repeating what the Prosecution has written in their stead. In one of their documents the Prosecution says that some of the witnesses had requested such procedure. Of course, those poor people cannot even repeat all the things the Prosecution had written for them. They might be able to if I remind them. But just off the top of their heads to repeat 20 pages of false testimony, they can't do it. Those people are not very smart, one must say. They simply are not up to the task. Some cases -- in some cases some written statements may be indeed admitted into evidence as long as it's not too much, but if this turns into the prevailing practice here, then why would I examine such witnesses? This is just a thought. I haven't decided finally. Not long ago, the Prosecution first sent me their old pre-trial brief with a new date from June this year. Like, they are disclosing to me this pre-trial brief, it was disclosed to me a long time ago. Why? And then it found its way to the Internet, and then some days ago I get their new pre-trial brief and it's not complete. Why? Some footnotes were crossed out in black. It's not the final version of their pre-trial brief. The final version must be disclosed six weeks before the pre-trial conference. If a single word is crossed out in black, it's not the final version, and you will see at least three footnotes blacked out, maybe more. Those references form an integral part of the text. What kind of game is that? How am I supposed to respond to their pre-trial brief which is not final? In that pre-trial brief, the Prosecution again treats the crime base and other things in the same way as in the previous pre-trial brief, the crime base in Bosanski Samac, Brcko, Bijeljina. What does that mean? Is that a reversal to the old indictment? If so, then let them say so in so many words. The pre-trial brief may not deal with anything that is not contained in the indictment, the current indictment. The Prosecution are at a loss what to do with their own indictment. They recently filed a request to amend it. And then comes another submission of the Prosecution in which they abandon the idea of amending paragraph 5 of the indictment. What does that mean?? In June they want to amend it, now they don't want to amend it. How long can this go on? I just got used to the new version and now it's being changed again. You know what happened. I had a very long confidential conversation with my legal assistants. We discussed these changes to paragraph 5 at length. We noted that the Prosecution made a grave mistake. We even made fun of them on that account and that telephone conversation which was not supposed to be wire-tapped was obviously wire-tapped. Transcripts were made available to the Prosecution, and now they are hastily giving up the idea of amending paragraph 5. That's my only explanation. That's what must have happened although this was supposed to be a secure communication, my legal assistants are recording it. I can give you the recording so you can check what I'm saying. It's the recording of my own telephone communications, and I have the right to disclose it, to divulge it. It was on a secure telephone line from the detention unit. In one of the documents that was recently served on me, I read. It's a report on disclosure by the OTP, submission 240, dated 25th July 2007, I got it on 31st of July. In paragraph 4 says: "The OTP is informed that the printing of the following material is finalised and a selection is now being made of the relevant parts of the material that is to be submitted to the CLSS. The conference and language service section. So they don't want to disclose all the material to me. They intend to select what they believe is relevant and serve me only with that. What is that supposed to mean? They can't choose what is relevant in any document. They have to give me the entire document. I will choose what is relevant to me or not, not they. Everything has to be translated. That would be it. I hope I didn't speak at too great a length. That would be it in the briefest possible terms. I have thus presented a few of my own observations regarding the situation now that we are preparing for trial. Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Seselj. Ms. Dahl, Mr. Seselj has tackled a host of issues. You now have the floor to answer and of course I will take the floor after you have done so. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have to confess I'm a little concerned about Mr. Seselj's paranoia regarding his secure telephone conversations with privileged persons. We have no such transcripts. I'm also a little worried that that demonstrates forgetfulness on his part. Our change regarding paragraph 5 of the indictment was consequent upon his objection to the removal of that language from the indictment. He correctly pointed out that the prior Trial Chamber had requested the Prosecution to indicate the nature of its allegations against Mr. Seselj. In my review of the indictment it appeared to me that that language was legal argument that belonged properly in the pre-trial brief. I didn't see any harm in taking it out. I don't see any harm in leaving it in, and our response to his objection was to suggest that it should remain in the second amended complaint against him. There's utterly no basis for his allegation that we're listening in on his conversations which are privileged. If we could go into closed session for a moment, I will address his confusion as to the filing procedures regarding the pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I strenuously oppose moving into private session because the explanation is not appropriate. The explanation is not in keeping with the Rules of Evidence and Procedure. There is no reason to close this session. The session may be closed only in order to mention the names of protected witness or confidential documents. The method of disclosure is no grounds for closing the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, if I understand correctly, you would like to move to private session in order to deal with names that were taken out of the pre-trial brief which had to do with the protected witnesses. Is that the reason why you would like to move to private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, to discuss the confidential status of documents. If the pre-trial judge does not require an explanation of the changes that were made to the pre-trial briefs and the corrections then there's -- I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You would like only to deal with the fact that you struck off some parts in the pre-trial brief which was a public document; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not willing to discuss confidential filings in an open session. I don't think that's appropriate. And my concern is that Mr. Seselj's confusion as to the procedure demonstrates his inability to proceed in the absence of the assistance of legal counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. I have listened to Mr. Seselj with great care, and I did not see any confusion. On the contrary, I even concluded that as time goes by, the more he becomes an expert in terms of proceedings before this Tribunal. Therefore, I fail to see why or where there could be a confusion. There is no need for open session unless you want to mention the name of a protected witness, otherwise you have to answer him and answer the points that he raised. He said himself that he was not mentioning any protected witness by name.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: My concern arises out the confidential filings. Your Honour, I will not discuss them in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And these confidential filings, from memory, they have to do with the submissions you made, applications for protective measures for certain witnesses; Is that right? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Presently we're discuss the pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the pre-trial brief that I have in front of me has become a public document, since a public version thereof has been filed. It was filed on 31st of July, 2007. I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Mr. Seselj had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in this public document on some very few pages, you can see and some footnotes that were removed. Is that what you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm not sure what documents Mr. Seselj is referring to because we filed a public version of the pre-trial brief and then asked for previously filed versions to be moved into confidential status. I believe all of that has been accomplished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Please proceed. There's no reason to move into private session. We know that there is a pre-trial brief in existence. We know that there is confidential version of that brief, and there's also a public version of the same pre-trial brief. So please present your submissions on the basis of the public version of the pre-trial brief because we are still in public session, in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj received copies to show the differences between the public and the confidential version. And if he requires further information about the reasons we're sending him material, I would request that he simply sends me a letter and I will be happen to facilitate his understanding of the Prosecution's filings. He also made mention of the Babic testimony which is the subject of a motion under 92 quater on all of the transcripts relating to Mr. Babic's testimony with the registrar, and I believe it comes within their undertaking to have such submissions translated. With regard to our request for protective measures on Friday the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment, please. Let me immediately address what he said about Mr. Babic. I listened to what he had to say with great interest. Why did I do so? Well it so happens by pure chance that I was the judge who confirmed the indictment raised against Mr. Babic, so needless to say that when I found out that Mr. Babic committed suicide it was something that I found quite striking. Based on what Mr. Seselj has said, Mr. Babic testified in a number of cases, and he listed these cases. And based on what he is telling us, there are documents in relation to these testimonies, and he would like to have access to these documents. Why? He told us earlier on that since the Prosecution filed a motion for admission by the chamber of Babic's statements and testimonies in a number of trials, he, Mr. Seselj, should have access to all the documents related to the testimonies of Mr. Babic, and Mr. Seselj told us that he does not have these documents at his disposal. Have you yourself identified all the statements, all the testimonies of Mr. Babic, and have these documents been disclosed to Mr. Seselj? That's what matters here, because he is saying that he doesn't have some of these documents. Furthermore, he added something that's news to me. He said the following, that I'm not aware of the heart of the matter. But he said that Babic supposedly denied what he had said before. In other words, he had recanted. He denied what he had stated before. This might raise a problem if Mr. Seselj tell us that Mr. Babic recanted what he had said before, then we would need to know what he said when he said, I would like to go back on what I said earlier on, and then we would also need to know what he said before.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, it's quite correct if has recanted, that would be something we would of course disclose. I have never heard such a thing, however, and Mr. Seselj has made a number of accusations regarding Mr. Babic which I have not seen support for, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me ask the question to Mr. Seselj. Mr. Seselj, you said earlier on that Mr. Babic denied some of the statements he'd made. On what occasion was it when he testified in the Martic case? What case are you talking about? Because apparently Ms. Dahl is not aware of this and it's news to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, perhaps there was a problem with the interpretation. I was very clear and very accurate in the Serbian language. I stated that by virtue of the fact that he committed suicide during the course of his testimony in the Milan Martic case. Milan Babic refuted all the evidence he gave before that. The act of suicide is a way of denying it. He committed suicide while giving testimony. That is how I interpret the act of his suicide. I was very precise in the Serbian language. What it was interpreted like to you, I really don't know. In this other case when I did not mention the witness' name because the witness is still protected, the witness had served his sentence, returned home. On the surface it seemed that he lived peacefully for a couple of weeks, and then he committed suicide when he had no external reason for doing so. These are forms of refuting false evidence. That is my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, you're telling us that is your personal interpretation, you work on the basis that when someone commits suicide, by this very act, they put in question what they had said before committing suicide. But that's your own interpretation of the death of Babic and of the other individual who served his sentence, went home, back home, and committed suicide without any specific reason. That's your own interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's my interpretation. However, supported with a series of arguments that I have given in order to support it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, please proceed Ms. Dahl. Now we understand what it was all about with Mr. Babic, so please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I was turning to our request for protective measures. In view of your instructions on Friday regarding the order of witnesses, I would like to modify our request and adapt it to Friday's instructions. We would like the disclosure of those witnesses for whom we have sought delayed disclosure consequent upon the commencement of trial to be modified so that disclosure is delayed until a reasonable period before their appearance at trial. When we discussed that on Friday, Your Honour had suggested that because the witnesses had waited this long before testifying, it wouldn't matter if they had to wait a little bit longer to come to give their evidence. The delay in there their presentation of testimony is not the source of concern. It's the length of time that their identity is closed that puts them at risk, and we'd like to make sure that we have adequately addressed their security risks. And I would like to follow the suggestions you had regarding the presentation of our evidence and propose that delaying disclosure until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, you indeed filed a motion for protective measures in relation to a number of witnesses. I'm not going to give their names or their reference numbers. The Defence in the person of Mr. Seselj responded for each witness to your submissions. I have spent a great deal of time working on this particular matter, and the Chamber or myself -- well, I am to deliver a decision on this matter in the near future, within two weeks, because most of the work has already been carried out. We are therefore currently in the process of finalising this decision. You're just telling me that following the Status Conference of Friday, the work plan then that I submitted to you, you had decided to adopt it, to agree with it, and that witnesses who were mentioned in paragraph (e) will now be heard at the end of the case.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, it's paragraph I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore we'll first have witness related to the crimes committed in various municipalities. I take note of this with great satisfaction, we are going the right way. But you are telling us something else. You're telling us that from your point of view, and of course that's not the position shared by Mr. Seselj, you're saying that you would like some -- the identity of some of the protected witnesses to be disclosed to Mr. Seselj only later, only one month before these witnesses come to testify, and not as Mr. Seselj would like it to be, and not one month before the beginning of the trial. On Friday, I told you that I believe that the trial should begin at the beginning of November. That would mean that the list of these witnesses and their identity should be disclosed to Mr. Seselj at the latest during the first week of October. But once -- when the trial started in this case last year, the Trial Chamber, with Judge Orie as Presiding Judge, took a decision in relation to protected witnesses. They took a decision about the time when these witnesses were to testify. And if I remember correctly, I might be mistaken of course - and if that's the case, the Chamber's legal officer will correct me immediately - but from memory, I believe that Trial Chamber I decided that the list of all these witnesses should be disclosed to Mr. Seselj at the beginning of the trial and not at the time when the witnesses come and testify. On this particular issue, Ms. Dahl, can you please shed some light for me?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: My recollection of the prior rulings was there was no such ruling to disclose all witnesses to Mr. Seselj at the commencement of the trial. If that were the case, we would have no more requests for delayed disclosure that are presently pending. I appreciate the amount much work that the Chamber is putting into addressing the protective measures requested in this case. I can give you a short list of the affected witnesses. But what I propose rather than moving all of the witnesses in category I to the back of the case is to, on an individual basis, determine where they fit in with the remaining crime base witnesses, if that's appropriate, to make sure that Mr. Seselj has a reasonable amount of time to prepare for their examination. The point is to balance the security risks with giving the accused proper and fair disclosure of the identity of the witnesses against him. We wanted to bring those witnesses for whom we had sought delayed disclosure in first, because that way the security risks are minimised, their evidence is put out as soon as possible, and we get past that hurdle in the case. I want to avoid overloading the accused with a large amount of new information and would propose, therefore, to time the delayed disclosure with their appearance at trial rather than the commencement of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge I'm really worried about this paranoia displayed here by Ms. Dahl in relation to alleged security risks for some witnesses. For most witnesses in fact, her lack of knowledge of the case file to date shows that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me interrupt you, Mr. Seselj. We are going to move into a private session, and I'll tell you why. Mr. Registrar, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in private session, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please, Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me just back up for just a second. On the disclosure of witnesses, there was ordinary entered on 8 November 2006 that directed the Prosecution to disclose the identity of all the witnesses relating to the Hrtkovci crime base, and that was done. That was the first crime base that we were leading testimony on when starting trial commenced last year, and of course it's the first that we would proceed upon this year. With regard to the exhibits we are doing our best to eliminate duplicates, and when the items were reordered into chronological order, taking them out of the logical relevance in which they had been ordered previously, there is a certain amount of duplication. I understand, Mr. Seselj's objections to relate primarily to relevance. Those are more properly addressed during trial when we seek to admit material. If there are duplicates that are unnecessary or not relevant in and of themselves, they will not be tendered. But we're doing our very best to get the material printed, properly labelled, and produced so that he has all of the material that will be shown in Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Dahl. Mr. Seselj, earlier on you mentioned something. I'd like to provide some information on this item. You said that witnesses who were not educated or did not have any knowledge had made statements, statements that were taken by the Office of the Prosecutor, and then the witnesses had signed their statements in English. And later on, according to you, those witnesses are going to challenge the contents of such statements. I'm going to be very precise in telling you how investigations are carried out. The Office of the Prosecutor meets with a witness, with a potential witness, whatever their name. You have the investigators of the OTP and a potential witness. So there are conversations between them, conversations that sometimes take days. Sometimes they're lengthy conversations over several hours, if not days. And following the discussions that take place between investigators and -- investigators and potential witnesses, there is a written statement by the witness. It is then drafted, and you're quite right in saying that it is a statement that is drafted by the OTP. The OTP writes a statement that is supposed to be a perfect match to what the witness said. The witness statement is then drafted in English, when the investigators use English, sometimes there are statements in French, but there are very few of them. Most of the time they are in English. The witness will sign the statement in English. But as a rule, the OTP will have the statement re-read, the English statement to the witness. There is an interpreter working into B/C/S. That interpreter will translate the contents of the English statement to the witness. Therefore, the witness will be listening to the interpreter as they interpret the statement as signed by the witness. That's the way it works. This is the evidence that is produced before this Tribunal. When you have a viva voce witness, there is a written statement that you have, that the OTP has, that the Trial Chamber has received the information. But it's not adduced into evidence, at least when you have a viva voce witness. The written statement, the prior statement, is not adduced. What you have then is only the transcript, and the transcript encompasses all the answers provided by the witness to answers put to him or her by the Prosecution, but also answers to the Defence questions in cross-examination. The witness statement is therefore not admitted into evidence. However, should there be a 92 bis motion, and should the motion be admitted, the written statement is then admitted into evidence. Now, when it comes to the 92 ter proceedings, you have the witness. They come to testify, they confirm the written statement in answer to a question by the Prosecution that asks whether the witness, were he to answer the same question as the ones put to them at the time of the written statement, and whether their answers would be the same, and if the answer by the witness in court is yes, then the written statement is admitted into evidence. Therefore, with regard to your rights as an accused, when you have viva voce witnesses, the written statement is totally irrelevant because what matters are the answers to questions in Court. If you have a 92 ter proceeding, then you can challenge what the witness may say in relation to their witness statement because you are free to ask them questions. However, if you have a Rule 92 bis, notwithstanding the fact that you put your comments in writing prior to the Trial Chamber's decision, once the decision is taken, the written statement is admitted into evidence. There's one thing have you to understand. In the investigation stage, the witness meets with representatives of the OTP, and the written statement, the prior statement that is the outcome of such meetings, is a summary of all this time spent on meetings between the investigators, members of the OTP, and witnesses. So I have listened to you with great care, and I do understand your concerns, your misgivings. It's true when a witness comes to testify, it may that be he doesn't remember what he said 14, if not 15 years ago. He may say the opposite of what he said in this prior statement. That can happen. But there are questions put in Court and they make it possible to see what the witness has to say, either as a result of the examination-in-chief or of cross-examination or as a result of the Judge's questions. So in this respect, I just wanted reassure you and to give you these explanations. Admittedly, at times, witnesses in Court do not say the same as what they may have said as when they were heard before. That can happen because they have thought it over or because they've changed their minds or because they've forgotten or they may also add on other things. So that can happen. However, the good thing about cross-examination is that you then can really reconstruct what the witness really said within the overall framework of their testimony. I just wanted to say this to you. Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, perhaps it's a major problem that I am so well versed in the methodology of work of the OTP. Basically the Prosecution calls two types of witnesses, victims and eye witnesses, and participants in events. Usually participants in events are told that they are potential suspects. According to the internal rules of the OTP, in that case the entire interview has to be video taped. Very often these video tapes are not made. Questions put by the investigators are leading questions very often and afterwards this statement is modified in accordance with the interests of the Prosecution. Now, what's the problem here? The Prosecution prepares each and everyone of their witnesses, like the Defence does. The Defence sometimes proof -- the Prosecution sometimes proof their witnesses for days. They prepare questions for them. They prepare questions that will be put in the examination-in-chief, the witness has an opportunity to learn the content of his alleged statement very well. Yet they're still afraid to brings witnesses like to that into the courtroom and to have them

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: learning all the answers that they're supposed to give. So then basically want to have statements admitted into evidence. And then what I do, I do through cross-examination questions in cross-examination, the interest of justice has to be carried out. It is in the interest of justice that all witnesses be heard viva voce and that they be examined by the Prosecutor in the courtroom. Let them make an effort in this respect. I'll give you a concrete example. VS-17 was a protected witness envisaged last year as the main and first witness that would be heard in my case. Just before the trial was supposed to begin, the Prosecution asked to have his statement admitted into evidence according to Rule 92 ter. They considered him an insider, a key witness, of course I will have ample opportunity to challenge this and to fully annul this statement, this testimony, through good arguments. But why? They are aware of all the problems that his testimony can have. They were his nature, his social behavior, his habits. They themselves gave me documents showing that he was a drinker and so on. They are afraid to examine this witness directly here. They would like to bring him in. They would like him to confirm that the statement taken by the investigator is his own, and then they'll see how he will fair during the cross-examination. They're counting on many other cases until now, that what mattered was the 92 bis statement and the cross-examination could be neglected. That is the way the OTP works, and that is why Ms. Dahl comes here with a request to have statements by an enormous number of witnesses admitted into evidence. If it were four or five witnesses that could perhaps be understandable and justified, but the tendency of the Prosecutor is to treat most witnesses that way. That is impermissible. Then this trial would turn into a farce before it even starts. Then one wonders what the point is of my participation in the proceedings. Perhaps I had better play a passive role, perhaps I just sit this thing out here. They'll force me to do that if they continue insisting on such an enormous number of witnesses that would be heard according to 92 bis, ter, and quater if by sometimes the Trial Chamber grants their request. In the spirit of rules and according to the Statute, witnesses should be heard viva voce. The rule provides for exceptions too, but not the majority of witnesses can be heard under exceptional circumstances 92 bis, ter, and quater are just exceptions to the rules that can be seen from the entire rules. If the entire trial is going to be based on rules that I envisaged for exceptions, then this is certainly going to be a very exceptional trial, but in a negative sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding what you have just said, let me give you some explanations in order to do away with any kind of ambiguity. You have a witness list, and you said it yourself, there are in that list so-called insider witnesses; in other words, witnesses who are going to speak to facts that are likely to put you as an accused in a situation of liability. In all Courts, in criminal Courts, major witnesses come to testify. There's no proceedings by written statement. Witnesses do come to testify in Court. Therefore, major Prosecution witnesses are going to be in Court. What you fear is the 92 ter type of proceedings. Here, too, I'd like to give you some explanations. When the Prosecution plans the testimony of a witness under Rule 92 ter, there is prior to this a motion that is filed with the Trial Chamber, and Rule 92 ter makes it possible for the Defence, therefore for you, to cross-examine the witness. Therefore, you were mentioning Witness VS-17, if the Prosecution were planning to have him as a 92 ter, you would be free to cross-examine him. You could then, in putting questions to him, challenge what he may have said, and your rights would be fully protected. Regarding Rule 92 bis, you know that is the Trial Chamber that takes rulings on 92 bis witnesses, and normally I should be one of the Judges on the merits, practice in this Tribunal as such that when there is a Prosecution motion under Rule 92 bis, and if the 92 bis provisions are complied with, a written statement may be admitted. But very often, and I would say nearly all the time, when an accused states that he wants to cross-examine a Rule 92 bis witness, the Trial Chamber then decides that the witness whose prior statement was to be admitted under Rule 92 bis should come to court for cross-examination. So this is not something that happens automatically. There is no written proceedings that would run against your own interests. You have an absolute right to cross-examine 92 ter witnesses and to move for cross-examination of 92 bis witnesses. The only exception to all this is the case of a witness who is deceased, who therefore inevitably cannot be cross-examined. In such a case, the Prosecution will file a motion for their testimony to be admitted into evidence. So this is the way things work. Mr. Seselj, you were telling us that if all this is admitted, you're not going to cross-examine. No. If there is a motion filed by the Prosecution for a 92 ter proceeding, the Prosecution's starting point is that there is a written statement. It is confirmed by the witness in court together with some documents. But thereafter you are free to cross-examine the witness, just as if it had been a viva voce witness altogether. There is no difference. You mentioned the interests of justice. You're quite right in doing so. There were cases in this Tribunal in which, in the interest of justice, written statements were admitted with no cross-examination. As far as I can remember, there was even a case - I couldn't give you the exact name - but there was a case, it was a trial here before this Tribunal, and a witness was heard; although, the accused and his counsel were not in Court. That was in the interest of justice. And you're also right in saying that the interest of justice principle must be justified and reasoned. There may be exceptional circumstances in which the interest of justice is higher than the interest of an individual or a party or a specific interest. Moreover, as I know that you read each and every word, you must have seen that the Plenary meetings of the Judges amended Rule 75 lately. And that has to do with protective measures for witnesses. Because of the interest of justice, it is now possible not to ask for the consent of a witness for protective measures to be lifted, protective measures that had been granted to that witness so that's already enshrined in the Rules. But as far as you are concerned, in our case, the case that we will have to deal with, I can't see which are the written statements the Prosecution would seek to admit without you knowing about it, without you being able to cross-examine the witness, without you being able to convey your point of view to the Trial Chamber. I don't think that is possible. Admittedly, and Ms. Dahl said that repeatedly, there will be motions for admission of written statements or testimony in prior trials, be it only yours, let's start with that. When you testified in the Milosevic case, also motions regarding Mr. Babic who is now deceased, of course you cannot cross-examine him, there will be a number of such mentions, but you have a right and that right will remain and will not be violated. Because even in Mr. Babic's case, you, through your submissions, you can change what he said. All this will be reviewed by the Trial Chamber who will assess all of the evidence. So this is what I wanted to tell you. In order to dispel any possible fears, fears that you may have and that you show sometimes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, the point of my opposition is the following, and I will be as simple as possible in stating my thoughts now. The point of my opposition is the following. Out of a total of 102 Prosecution witnesses, how many witnesses can be heard according to 92 bis/ter? The tendency displayed by the OTP is to have most witnesses heard according to 92 bis, ter, and quater. Is that acceptable or not? In my opinion that is quite unacceptable. Witnesses that are heard according to 92 bis, quater, and ter can only be exceptions. There can only be a few exceptions in relation to the total of 102 witnesses. That is the essence of my opposition to this. If most witnesses here will be 92 bis ter, and quater witnesses, then there will be no trial. Then it is going to be a trial in absentia. Then it is going to be a Kafkaesque trial in the true sense of the word. An enormous majority of witnesses have to be heard viva voce. Only exception can be heard 92 bis, ter, and quater. If it is the other way around, then it would be inadmissable from the point of view in the interest of justice. That is my view. Of course I know that some witnesses will have to be 92 bis, ter, or quater witnesses but not most of the witnesses. And you see how they have prepared this, that most witnesses should be heard in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I will respond to this and Ms. Dahl will probably do so as well. We need to have a break now, but after the break, I'll deal with the matter of the length of the Prosecution case and Defence case, and all the things that have been said up until now will then be taken into account. We will have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. The hearing is resumed, and I'm now going to deal with a matter that is in direct line with the submissions made by both parties so far. Mr. Seselj stated that the Prosecution intends to call 102 -- between 102 and 105 witnesses, and he stated that he wants to cross-examine all of these witnesses. This matter will only be resolved once the Trial Chamber has set the time allocated to the Prosecution to present their case. You know, of course, that it is during the pre-trial conference that will take place right before the beginning of the trial, that's when the Trial Chamber makes that particular decision. As far as I'm concerned personally, I'm not in a position to rule on the matter and to state that the Prosecution will be granted so many hours to put their case. But it's true, I don't have that power, but I'm still free to express my feelings about this, and my feeling in that respect is as follows. If we look at the list of the Prosecution witnesses, we see that we have about 100 witnesses listed by the Prosecution so far. The Prosecution has not made a distinction between viva voce witnesses, 92 ter, 92 quater, or 92 bis witnesses. Once the Prosecution has completed that exercise, inevitably they won't have as many viva voce or 92 ter witnesses. The number will be much smaller. How could the Prosecution go about this, go about preparing the witness list? There are two parameters the Prosecution needs to take into account. The first factor, the first parameter, is the fact that 81 hours had been granted to the Prosecution to put its case by the Trial Chamber presided by Judge Orie. That's the lower option. If we look at the higher one, we are looking at a calculation I made with my assistants by adding up all the time stated in the 65 ter list for the 102 to 105 witnesses, and by adding all this time up, we came up with a total of 269 hours. Admittedly, everybody agrees that we won't have 100 witnesses who will come and testify. Therefore, the Trial Chamber will have to set a time which will be between 81 and 269 hours. In my opinion, and that's the position I will defend before my colleagues, in my opinion, 100 hours should be granted to the Prosecution, and that would be plenty, in my opinion. Why 100 hours? Well, for the following reason. We will be sitting three days a week. Being the Presiding Judge and sitting -- and since I would be sitting in another trial, I would not be in a position to sits in this case for three days a week. And further more that's what has been requested by Mr. Seselj himself to put his case properly. We work on the basis that we'll be sitting on Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday of each week. Therefore, we'll have, in total, ten hours of hearing per week, ten hours of actual hearing time. If you multiply this by four weeks, you come up with a total of 40 hours each month. If we grant 100 hours to the Prosecution to put their case, Mr. Seselj will automatically be granted 100 hours for cross-examination purposes. As a result, during the Prosecution case, we should work on the basis of 200 hours. In other words, five months of hearing. Five months, because that will be 40 hours a month -- a week, and in total 200 hours in five months. When we begin with the Defence case, if Mr. Seselj has the same number of witnesses, and if he also needs 100 hours to hear his witnesses, the Prosecution will be granted 100 hours as well, and will need an additional five months, five months in total for the Defence case. As a result, if we are not faced with any major problems, we should be able to complete this case within one year. But in order to achieve this, we need to resolve all procedural matters that are bound to slow down any trial. As far as I'm concerned personally, I'd rather dedicate my time to reviewing witness statements and exhibits rather than wasting time on matters of procedure that, in any case, will not come to bear on the decision of whether to acquit or to convict the accused. But for this, we need to prepare the trial properly, and that's why I've been trying over the past few months to deal with all the problems as soon as they come up. I realise that I'm gradually getting there, because on Friday I was in a position to tell the Prosecution that all witnesses listed under I were to be moved at the end of their case and the Prosecution this morning told me that they were amenable to this. In other words, we are moving ahead. We are moving forward and in a positive manner. To conclude on this time issue, Ms. Dahl, you should immediately start to take the following into account. You should think out of these 100 hours, how many hours you want to dedicate to fact witnesses, how many hours you want to use with expert witnesses, how many hours you want to dedicate to what we call insider witnesses, and to also to the main witnesses. You have to take into account that some witnesses may be heard under 92 bis. If they corroborate or confirm what other witnesses have said, but it will be up to the Trial Chamber to rule on this. Of course you have to keep -- bear in mind that Mr. Seselj may ask for some of these 92 bis witnesses to come here for him to cross-examine them. As a consequence, Ms. Dahl, I would like to invite you to work on the basis of 100 hours that. That -- and at that time may be shorter or longer depending on what my fellow Judges decide, because I will not be alone in making that decision. The two other or the other Judges sitting on the Trial Chamber will also have their say when we rule on this matter. But I believe that a total of 100 hours would appropriate. We would be able then to sit three days a week, and we would be working on the basis of Prosecution case that would last five months. These are the comments I wanted to make at this stage of the proceedings with respect of time. This is of course a matter relevant to the Prosecution in the first instances. Therefore, Ms. Dahl, do you want to say asking about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour. It seems like a very sensible way to proceed, and I wanted just to clarify that our accession to reordering the presentation of witness within category I is conditional on modification of our motion for protective measures. I have a short list of the effective witnesses that I will supply after today's proceedings. We will see whether those witnesses are more properly brought at the end of the case or if their relevance makes it appropriate to bring them within the different crime bases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Seselj, we are talking about 100 hours for the Prosecution. That would mean 100 hours for you to cross-examine the Prosecution witnesses, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I believe this is a very reasonable evaluation, 100 hours for the Prosecution and 100 for me for cross-examination. One should take into account that I will insist on the same time for experts and Defence witnesses. Of course, including my own testimony, which would last ten, 15, maybe even 20 days because I referred to the experience of Krajisnik. Mr. Krajisnik testified for 40 days, 23 days in chief, 12 days for cross and some days for redirect. I will give a great deal of attention to that in the process of preparing my Defence. However, there is another problem. I believe it's quite unrealistic for the Prosecution to lead 100 or 102 witnesses in 100 hours. For the past three Status Conferences I insist on getting an answer to the question why the list of witnesses includes witnesses for crime base on Western Slavonia, Samac, Brcko, and Bijeljina and why the crime base in those areas is dealt with in the pre-trial brief if those locations have been deleted from the indictment? There might be a possibility here for saving time and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... You're absolutely right. You mentioned the fact on Friday, and I'm glad you raise it again today. Ms. Dahl, has already mentioned this point. He saw that in the new indictment some locations have been deleted. However, we still have witnesses on the list who normally should not come and testify, because the locations they would be testifying about have been deleted from the indictment. How do you explain this?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I would refer Mr. Seselj to the decision of 8 November 2006 that allowed the Prosecution the discretion to call witnesses relating to those municipalities under limited circumstances. I will consider carefully the Pre-Trial Judge's observations regarding how much time to dedicate to the various kinds of witnesses, who are the main ones, who are the insiders, who are the experts, and who are the particular fact witnesses. And it may be that the need to present pattern evidence will recede when we are confronted with 100 trial hours. But that is really within our discretion to figure out what is the appropriate weight of the evidence. I appreciate Mr. Seselj's observation about how we should prove our case but that is for us to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. But please take this matter into account. First of all, with regard to the decision taken on the 8th of November, 2006, it's a decision that was taken by the previous Trial Chamber. I'm not in a position to tell you whether the following Trial Chamber will follow the same logic. As far as I'm concerned, and it's my personal opinion, if -- the way I see it, if municipality have been deleted from the indictment, it's not necessarily relevant to have the witnesses come and testify about these municipalities. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully agree. One should bear in mind that you have before you the motion to accept the second amended indictment. I believe that's the official name. Possible admission, confirmation of that second amended indictment makes the decision of the previous Trial Chamber from November of last year irrelevant, because it applied to the modified amended indictment. The crime base has been deleted from it, but it was said that Prosecution may lead evidence on that pattern of conduct. I believe that was the formation. However, since this is no longer mentioned in the indictment at all, the question arises why some other places could not be included, a whole number of other places, 30, 40, 50 other locations. But the possibility to lead evidence on patterns of conduct does not mean that they can lead evidence on crime base, so the behaviour of the Prosecution is not consistent here. In any case, I believe the Prosecutor has to work on a new pre-trial brief. That pre-trial brief must be disclosed and it must not contain material on any municipality that is not mentioned in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are giving the opportunity to deal with a matter I wanted to address and that is the matter of the pre-trial brief. This is a very important point for you, Mr. Seselj. Please listen carefully. I know that you're always listening, but please pay particular attention what I'm going to say now about the pre-trial brief. In July, the Prosecution established or drew up its amended pre-trial brief, different from the one dated -- from June. Therefore, the consolidated pre-trial brief is dated from the month of July. I have read through this brief with great interest. It's a document that is very important for you, Mr. Seselj. What is a pre-trial brief? The pre-trial brief is an indictment but an indictment that has been detailed, analysed, and it's a document where all the arguments of the Prosecution are being developed, just as I have done, I'm quite sure you've reviewed this pre-trial brief, and you haven't failed to notice that in this brief we find first an introduction, and then various chapters. We have a chapter dedicated to your participation of the joint criminal enterprise in three respects. First of all as a promoter of greater Serbia; then, as a recruit and coordinator of the SRS volunteers; and thirdly, as a participant in the joint criminal enterprise. Then we find the implementation of the JCE in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia. In chapter 4 we have a chapter dedicated to the SRS structure, its structure, its organisation, and then in the following chapter we have the alleged crime in Croatia, in Bosnia, in Serbia, and in the following chapter of the pre-trial brief we find legal review under Article 7(1), as well as under Articles 3 and 5 of the same statute. In this pre-trial brief, you find all the arguments raised by the Prosecution with footnotes telling you which witnesses will confirm what is written in this pre-trial brief. What will happen next? When the Prosecution put their case, they will first start on the first day by giving a summary of the pre-trial brief. Then the Prosecution will call their witnesses in the order we mentioned on Friday. But this order will follow the order adopted in the drafting of the pre-trial brief. Therefore, this is a document of utmost importance for you, Mr. Seselj. Why is it so? It is so because once the Judges have to rule on your liability, on your responsibility, once they have to pass judgements on the crimes that were committed, they will have to rule on the basis of all the evidence adduced at trial. In the judgment and you know that as well as I do, in the judgement, as in all other judgements, in the trial judgement, Judges always refer to the pre-trial brief as well as to the brief produced by the accused in response to the Prosecution pre-trial brief. Rule 65 ter (F) states the following. Let me read it out to you very slowly. I quote: "After the submission by the Prosecutor of the items mentioned in paragraph (E)," in other words, and must read the pre-trial brief, "the Pre-Trial Judge shall order the Defence," in other words you, Mr. Seselj, "within a time-limit I will set, and not later than three weeks before the pre-trial conference to file pre-trial brief addressing the factual and legal issues and including a written statement setting out in general terms the nature of the accused's Defence, the matters with which the accused takes issue in the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief, and in the case of each such matter, the reason why the accused takes issue with it." In other words, you and your associates have to do that work, and you have to produce your own pre-trial brief for the Trial Chamber in response to the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, in which you will challenge, because you've pleaded not guilty, in which you will change the case put forward or put forth by the Prosecution. You may do so, but you may choose not to do so. But I'm telling you one thing, Mr. Seselj. If you decide not to carry out that exercise, this could prove to be a handicap for you, because we are working here according to a procedure that is very different than what you're familiar with in your own country. In your country - and I know that - unfortunately for you, you have been convicted, you were convicted in the past, and you know that in continental rights system, law system, once the witnesses have testified at trial, the Prosecution make their final submissions, and the Defence make their final statement to refute what has been said by the Prosecution, sometimes also with briefs being produced. But here it's different. We have a pre-trial brief, we have witnesses who come and testify, then we have the Defence who have to -- to produce a document where they challenge the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. You -- it is not compulsory for you to prepare a pre-trial brief, but if you decide not to do so, once the Judges assess all the evidence produced at trial, they will only have at their disposal the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, the transcript of the witnesses's testimonies, and the exhibits. I believe that a pre-trial brief that would you produce in response to the Prosecution's brief could prove to be extremely valuable. I have listened-- or have read rather with great interest, all the submissions you and your associates have produced in response to the various expert reports. What you have done with respect to the expert witnesses, you could do it again, in my opinion, to respond to the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. But we are starting to run out of time here because taking into account the three-week time limit before the beginning of the trial, this particular document should be completed by the 10th of October. Today is the 20th of October [as interpreted], we will still have the month of September and the month of October. You have two months to complete that work. I don't know what you intend to do, Mr. Seselj. Are you going to prepare a brief or not? I would like to know what is your position about this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I have decided to file a Defence pre-trial brief in any case, and I'm already working on it in order to respond to the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. However, the Prosecution has still not given me the final version of their pre-trial brief, which they are required to do under Rule 65 ter (E) line 1. The final version of the pre-trial brief cannot be a version in which something is blacked out, even the minimal. The final version of the pre-trial brief has to be an integral one. Somebody mentioned a moment ago that there is a confidential and a public version of the pre-trial brief. I received only the public one. I don't have the confidential version. It hasn't been served on me, since it has not, then I don't have the final version of the pre-trial brief. Maybe the Prosecution will give it to me tomorrow, but you have obviously to instruct them to do so because they will not do so otherwise. I will look at the deadlines envisaged by the rules, and I will file my own pre-trial brief a little earlier perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this respect, in the issue of the confidential pre-trial brief versus the public version, what do you have to say to Mr. Seselj? Because he needs the final version of the pre-trial brief, that's obvious, for him to be able to answer, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Of course he does Your Honour. We're in complete agreement. As far as I know there is no reason why he should not have both copies. I submitted them both to be served on him and as far as I know the registrar submitted the full version to the conference and language services. I provided as much information in electronic form to the interpreters to facilitate the translation. So I will look into it and make sure that it's been served on him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj, Ms. Dahl is in full agreement with you. You should have the document as translated in your own language. Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So much the better, Judge, if Ms. Dahl agrees. But it is inconceivable to me that I have to wait so long. If only small passages are blacked out. It's not a big problem for the CLSS. It can be done in minutes. It's not about descriptions. It's some information that may not even be necessary in translation. I think it's an excuse that the CLSS is the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. There is a pre-trial brief, in which some parts were blacked out. It's enough to format the document so that all the parts in black be removed and that's it. All the problems are solved. If you have the pre-trial brief before you, look at page 29, for instance. There is a footnote there, a statement of and then something is blacked out, and then the text continues. Maybe you have to adjust some things but that can be done easily very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: May I ask Your Honour to tell me what is the document identification number in the upper right-hand corner, because I'm puzzled we didn't file the pre-trial brief of June with any redactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 21968, page 29, upper right corner, 21968.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: If I may suggest, Your Honour, that we proceed with what may remain on today's agenda. I will make sure that the proper documents are served on Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, let me deal with a very important issue, a question which is bound to arise at trial. We have mentioned this briefly before, but without going into detail, into technical details. I have in mind the issue of proofing in English, recollement in French. What happens in this respect? Mr. Seselj, let us imagine that there is a witness who is due to testify on Tuesday, because that's the first day, that will be our first day of hearing. If this is a major witness, it is likely that he or she will arrive earlier, will arrive before the weekend, so he or she will spend the weekend and Monday here. Proofing is a procedure which are you familiar with, because you spoke about it yourself in which the Prosecutor meets with their witness prior to the hearing in order to speak with the witness about the written statement, because the written statement may have been drafted many years before. The witness is then shown documents which are going to be put to him at trial in court. And there's some kind of training that takes place in order to prepare the witness for testimony. During this preparation, it may happen, and I would say that it nearly always happens, that the witness may wish to make some changes to the statement he made several years before. Let me take a very simple example. Several years before, he may have said that most of the houses in his village had been destroyed, and then on the day when he comes to meet with the Prosecutor he will say, Well, that's what I said then but I was wrong. There was only about 30 per cent of the houses that were destroyed, it's not quite the same. So this is a new factor that comes into play. The Prosecutor is under the obligation to notify you of that straight away without delay. Equally, when they meet with the witness, the Prosecution had not planned to produce a document, and they realise that they now need the said document, which you did not have in the initial list. The Prosecutor is under the obligation of informing the accused that they plan to produce in court a new document. What is the problem? Let's say that the hearing begins on Wednesday morning at 9.00 in the morning. The Prosecution will meet with the witness on Tuesday at 5.00 in the afternoon. They have a meeting with the witness until 11.00 at night, which is not just theoretical because it is often the way it happens. At 11.00 p.m., the Prosecutor has to inform you that changes have been made to the witness's statement and that are there new documents. It is 11.00 at night. You are in your cell fast asleep. The hearing will begin the next morning at 9.00. If you were to have a counsel, the counsel is the one who is informed. As you know, counsel works 24 hours a day, so no problem there. But you, you are in your cell. It's 11.00, you're asleep, and you must be informed of these new factors prior to the hearing which is due to begin at 9.00 a.m because you must be informed and possibly you must be able on Wednesday to conduct your cross-examination. So I really thought this over very thoroughly. What can we do? The only solution, and I've really looked into this, the only solution would be to put into the cell that serves as your library to put a fax machine, which is directly connected to the Prosecution, to the OTP, so that if the Prosecutor had to tell you something at 11.00 at night, they can send a fax. You know there are silent fax machines so you won't be woken up, but as you said last time, you get up at 4.00 in the morning, so no problem there. You can find, at dawn, you can find the new changes made to the witness's statement, you can find the new documents, and you can prepare for the hearing starting at 9.00. Indeed, if the Prosecutor has a new document, that document will be faxed to you as well so you have everything in hand arriving by fax. Of course nobody thought about this problem, but I -- I am a professional and, as such, I have come across this type of problem in other cases before this Tribunal when there are accused or counsel who create problems because they say they have not been informed of changes recently made. So this is the way to go about it so that you are not taken unawares. This is a major problem because that's the result of the proofing session. So, Ms. Dahl, would that be a problem? Could you inform Mr. Seselj should this come up? Can you inform him?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: If he needs immediate notice, that sounds like a very sensible solution. I prefer not to work at 11.00 at night, but sometimes that's unavoidable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, now you've got all the parameters. What do you think of this? It is a technical matter, but it goes to the very heart of your right as an accused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would be bothered by being woken up at 11.00 p.m., but I don't mind between 4.00 ran 5.00 a.m. I'm not sure the detention authorities will technically be able to install a fax machine in my cell. That would be a good solution, but I don't know what their capacities are. Although there is a telephone set close to my cell, there could be a possibility of getting a line into my cell that would involve some additional construction works. I remember Mr. Milosevic had practically an office inside the DU, and he had a telephone and a fax there. If that could be placed within my cell, then I wouldn't need an office, and I suppose that would save resources to the DU. But I hope those cases would be rare, and they would not surprise me with urgent documents too often, because I need time to prepare my response to those amended and modified documents. It's not just a question of familiarizing myself but also of taking action to check that out, to find counterproof, counterevidence. Therefore, this is possible as an exception, but it shouldn't turn into a practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. But experience shows and that is experience that is most important. There are witnesses now, and they're going to be Prosecution witnesses, but you'll have your Defence witnesses too. The witnesses come and have a proofing session with the Prosecution or with the Defence if they are Defence witnesses. And sometimes witnesses come with documents. The Prosecution did not know anything about the existence of such documents, neither did the Defence, if they are Defence witnesses. And witnesses say, Well, look, six months ago I found this document. So there is the late discovery of documents that are sometimes very important. In this case, it is incumbent on the Prosecutor to inform the accused of such documents. Sometimes we have international witnesses who have notebooks in which they have recorded their entire lives. I mean, as part of their work, and they come and say, Look I've got my own log-book or my own notebook, and I make it available to you, but this is not something that they said to the investigator previously. So this is the type of problem that might come up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know. But in some other cases as well such problems occurred. However, if something of that kind happens, Judge, then the testimony of that witness must be delayed because that document must be translated into Serbian, especially if there is an international witness. Even there I will not accept anything in foreign languages. Defence council in other cases accepted such documents because they were required to know English; although, many of them just signed a statement saying that they knew English without actually knowing the language, and they were forced to accept such documents. In my case these documents have to be translated. Only translated can such documents be relevant for me and used in cross-examination. Until they are translated they practically don't exist, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Seselj has just raised an issue which is that if you have a document of this type but it's not translated, he's going to challenge it, and he wants that -- you know, the hearing of that witness to be stayed. There's one way of solving this problem: Don't wait until the very last minute to size up the problem. If you got in touch with such a witness some weeks before in order to see whether they have new documents and if they say, Yes, I have, it's a document in English, then you will ray have to make sure it is translated. Yes Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm in agreement of thinking ahead and planning. I would presume that Mr. Seselj would insist continually during trial for documents to be disclosed in his own language rather than assuming that he would shift from that position. While we have been in court, we have been checking on the service of the pre-trial brief in translation in its full and unredacted form, and I've located a process verbal showing that it was served on Mr. Seselj on 10 August. So I think that he has everything that he needs in complete format I was not aware that -- actually, not that I wasn't aware. There was nothing redacted from him in the confidential version that was served 10 August. The redactions are what was in the public version, and he was served with those pages to make sure he was informed fully of what was appearing in the record of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently, Mr. Seselj, a document was served on you on the 10th of August, a document was served on you, and from what Ms. Dahl says it should be the final version.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, that's absolutely not true. I signed receipt for every document.
