In August first I received the old pre-trial brief, then its supplement from 2003, or rather, 2005, whenever that supplement was made. And I was astounded to see they were serving it again. Then they served me with the new pre-trial brief with those passages left out. I never received a final version of the pre-trial brief. The Prosecution is in possession of all my receipts and so does the Registry. This is absolutely not true. But nobody can make it clear to me why they served me with the old pre-trial brief in the first place. Somebody seems to be trying to confuse me deliberately. I got the old pre-trial brief and its supplement, and then several days later I got the new pre-trial brief with those lines blacked out and that's the only thing I received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Seselj is telling us that as far as he knows the latest in pre-trial brief he received was one with [indiscernible]. So what's the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I will found out and make sure that he has what he needs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that. Mr. Seselj, I'm going return the three binders to you, and I'm going to address the issue you raised in relation to them. You complained that many documents were given to you and you did not see why they were relevant. You gave an example, that of JNA rules as to the command structure in the army. This is what you said. It may be that in your eyes that's not important or has no direct bearing on your case. But, you see, it could be relevant and I'll tell you why. If individuals can be accused of specific crimes, and if these individuals were dressed in uniforms, whatever they are, if they were wearing uniforms, they must be or have acted carrying out orders they have received, and there could be orders among the evidence. I don't know. I have not seen the documents yet. I'm just saying this as a mere hypothesis. If there were orders, the question is whether the orders were drafted on the basis of the then applicable rules within the former Yugoslav Army or applicable in the JNA or in the TO formations. If this is the case, to see whether the order was in keeping with the rules and regulations, the accused needs to have those rules and regulations. I guess this is the reason why the OTP disclosed all these documents to you. Admittedly, there are documents that are more or less relevant. Admittedly, in your eyes, and it may also be the point of view of the Trial Chamber, one can wonder whether certain documents are relevant or not. But there may be documents which do not appear to be relevant on day 1 of the trial. Well, those documents could be or seem relevant on day 81 of the trial. Therefore, all the documents disclosed to you under Rule 66 and under Rule 68, all the documents in the 65 ter list, are documents used to draft the indictment, and they also can be mentioned in the pre-trial brief. So before saying that certain documents are not relevant, you should look at them. But it is true that you risk being flooded with documents, and we are talking about tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of pages that have you to come to terms with. Maybe you are up to the task but you do have associates, and they are all worth looking into. You have received the binders from the Prosecutor. I have received them too. I think I have received at least 29 binders. I believe Ms. Dahl is going to send 150 of them in the next few day? Is that right? You still have another 120 or 30; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I believe we're making arrangements for delivering another batch this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Of course you need look at these binders. You will see there are lists, index lists, you will see that very quickly. So exhibit number 1 is easily dealt with. So you do that work, you're going to go through all the documents, see which are the essential documents to you and those that are not. This is what you're going to get. Because all the documents that will get to you in these binders are numbered 1 to 3.000 or 5.000, I can't remember, and they are the Prosecution's exhibits. But you know that when witnesses come to testify, you will get exhibit binders that will be submitted to the witness, and they will have exhibit numbers and you will have received the list beforehand. And on the day of their testimony, you'll get from the Prosecutor a binder with only those of the documents that are going to be put to the witness. But that's another stage of the proceedings. This is what I wanted to tell you regarding all the binders. Yes, Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, it occurred to me in considering the logistics in considering logistics of the difficulties that Mr. Seselj will have representing himself, how he will be able to transport his work product that he might need for a particular day in court back and forth with him. I mean, he won't exactly have a trolley for his notebooks, and I'd like to get some thought in advance to make sure that he has what he needs in the courtroom as well as in his house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. Ms. Dahl is telling you something that is important. You'll soon notice, Mr. Seselj, that when a witness comes to testify, the Prosecutor comes with a trolley, containing various binders, documents related to the witness but also related to other parts of the trial. So the Prosecution comes with their trolleys. I've worked on other trials here, and I see that Defence counsel also come with their trolleys. They're all equipped. When we have a self-representing accused, the only case I am aware of is that of Mr. Milosevic, he was representing himself and would cross-examine witnesses, I can't remember that he came with trolleys, I can't remember that very distinctly, but if you plan that for a particular witness, you'll have to make sure that your associates do prepare the necessary documents to make them available to you. Have you thought about this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I will prepare my own documentation myself, and I have always guards next to me who will have to carry that material because I am handcuffed throughout the transportation. So guards may have to undergo some harder physical training or maybe the guards can push the trolley. But there is something else that you said, judge, that is more important to me. The former Yugoslav People's Army published as an official manual for all soldiers, non-commissioned officers, and officers a collection of regulations of international humanitarian law, and none of the three categories, soldier and CO officer or politician can say that they didn't know something was prohibited under international laws of warfare. If something was done, then they knew while doing it that it was wrong, that it was prohibited by law, and that document, which the Prosecution served on me, of which I was aware even before because I had served in the army is sufficient. However, the rule of the corps is a matter concerning the strategy of warfare. It is learned in schools for generals or military academies. It deals not with international laws of warfare, just with military strategy, because a corps is a strategic unit. A brigade can be an operative or a strategic unit, a company is a tactical unit. So tactics, operations, strategy, and logistics are purely military disciplines that have nothing to do with international laws of warfare. I know in advance that the documents are not relevant because I am more qualified in this respect than the Prosecution. There is an even greater problem that I tried to point out at one of earlier Status Conferences. Those documents, in the understanding of the Prosecution, should be admitted into evidence. How are they going to be admitted into evidence if the Prosecution has only 100 hours to lead their evidence and 4.000 documents. Here in the courtroom, at least briefly, each of these documents has to be looked at and mentioned. I will use each of my documents that the guards will pull on a trolley. It's not the trolley that's the problem. It's the whole idea is inconceivable. It's impossible. This trial is conceived as a spectacular one. The Prosecution thought they would succeed in imposing Defence counsel on me and they were wrong. Now this whole spectacle is being reduced to a small trial, 100 hours for the Prosecution and 100 for the Defence and that's it. That amount of evidence cannot be pushed through within 200 hours, and I will not allow any document to be admitted into evidence without establishing myself, the link with the witness, and without the Prosecution explaining why that document is relevant. They have 4.000 documents, and they want to snow me under 150 binders. I don't know what to do with them. But what's going do be difficult is to admit all these documents into evidence, because I will question the relevance and authenticity of every document. They won't manage just to have them automatically have them admitted. The fact that this has gone on in other trials, in other cases, doesn't mean that it will work with me. Not a single document will be admitted into evidence before the Prosecution explain what in the document is relevant and before I am given the chance to question the relevance set aside even the questioning of witnesses. I don't know if Ms. Dahl has much experience in other cases, obviously she doesn't know much about the procedure and she needs a more capable assistant to explain to her the procedure, and to explain to her that she has to rationalise the Prosecution case and restrict the amount of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, apparently the Prosecution intends to use 4.000 documents, it might be less, it might be more, I'm not sure. For the time being, we do not know. The Prosecution have listed all the documents on that list according to what I requested. We have cross-references between these documents and the relevant paragraphs in the indictment. Therefore, the documents should be shown to be relevant because they relate to a specific paragraph of the indictment. In that list, you will see that one particular document may be related to various paragraphs of the indictment. In other words when a witness comes to testify, and that applies to all trials here, to the Milosevic trial, to all trials, the documents will be shown to the witness who might identify it or not. According to the case-law of this Tribunal, documents that are not known to the witness may be admitted into evidence. The Prosecutor may say, The following is stated in this particular document, do you agree, do you challenge this and so on and so forth. You yourself, as an accused, may, as part of your cross-examination, challenge this and tell the witness you said this in relation to this paragraph of the document, but in the other paragraph we see this and this. Therefore, a document is being looked at very thoroughly as part of the examination process. The document is also available to the Judges and they may ask questions on the basis of the documents. After that, the Prosecution will ask for the document to be admitted, and the Defence may challenge the admission. And it so happens that I wanted to deal with this particular issue. A document is admitted into evidence based on two criteria. The first one is the criterion of relevance; the second one, the second factor to be taken into account is probative value. Probative value must be rated zero plus to infinitum. But first we might have a document that is not very relevant and does not have a very high level of probative value but that does not mean that the Trial Chamber will automatically dismiss the said document. We might have a document that initially does not appear to be very relevant, but as with various witnesses coming and testifying, the document might appear to be much more relevant than at first thought. You have raised two issues just now. You raised the matter of the number of documents of you are telling us that the Prosecution will not have time to submit all the 4.000 documents in the 100 hours granted to them. Therefore, the Prosecution will only submit the most important documents that have been mentioned in the pre-trial brief in the footnotes. The major documents are mentioned in the pre-trial brief, all of them. These documents will be submitted to the witnesses. Other documents will also be shown to the witnesses. Since we are dealing with your case, but you have to remember that in other cases as well, thousands of documents are being submitted. According to the case-law of the Tribunal, if documents have not been submitted to a particular witness for -- because there was not enough time or because there were just too many documents, a written submission may be filed by the Prosecution for the admission of these documents afterwards, provided that the documents are relevant, have a probative value, and confirm, supplement, or corroborate what the witness has said or the -- what was said or written in other documents. The accused is free to accept or to dismiss the application. He makes his submissions in writing, and afterwards, the Trial Chamber rules on this matter. In other words, Mr. Seselj, out of these 4.000 documents listed by the Prosecution, the Prosecution may have only enough time to put to 1.000 or 2.000 documents to the witnesses, I'm not quite sure. If the Prosecution want to tender additional documents, they will file a written submission explaining why the documents have not been shown to the witnesses, why they want them to be admitted, et cetera. A number of decisions of that kind have already been issued in this Tribunal. The same will apply to you when you call your own witnesses. Let's imagine that you call 2.000 witnesses. You call the witnesses and 20.000 documents. You will have to make a selection, you will have to go for the most important documents. As for documents that are not that important but that you want to show to the Judges anyway, you will be in a position to file a written application asking for their admission. Why have we adopted this procedure? Well, it is because we are working in a system that is a mixture of common and continental law. What would have happened in my country, in your country? Well, as part of the investigation, all documents would have been -- would have been admitted into the file, into the case file. And then everyone, all the parties would have had access to the documents. But here, in this Tribunal, we are working according to the principles of common law when it comes to evidence. The Judges of the Tribunal, acting very wisely, have improved on the common-law system. They've accepted the admission of documents that have not been shown at trial. Because, as in the common-law system, documents are always admitted through a witness. But in common-law procedure when you -- when a cow thief is being tried, this thief is not being shown thousands of documents, of course. Here, this Tribunal, we are dealing with cases that involve a very large number of documents, and because of this large number of documents, it is not physically possible to have a look at all these documents, and since not all the documents can be shown, because if that was to be the case, we would need hundreds of years to complete the trials and we would all die before the end. A system -- a new system was needed, and the system that has been implemented in this Tribunal is that, as a general rule, documents are submitted and admitted through a witness, but when the -- there are too many documents and not enough time, documents may be admitted following a written application. The rights of the accused are fully complied with, because the accused may challenge the documents mentioned in the application. This is what I wanted to tell you with respect to the number of documents, because that might pose a problem to you, but the Chambers have solved the problem in the way I have just outlined. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, you mentioned wisdom, the wisdom of the Judges of this Tribunal. That wisdom is widely known throughout the world, and therefore what is combined in this Tribunal are the most negative elements of Anglo-Saxon and continental law. That is a well-known fact by now in law. In continental law, in civil law, it is the judge who checks the authenticity of the document and who is in charge of the investigation, whereas here it is the only the Prosecution that conducts an investigation. The Court does not have an opportunity to check the authenticity of documents unless witnesses are brought in that will confirm that. Recently a request was submitted by the Prosecution for notice regarding certain documents. I'm preparing a reply, and I am going to say that the only thing that can be received that way are official documents like Laws on Defence, Security, whatever else. I'm going to challenge anything, everything else. Stenographic notes where there is not reliable evidence that they are authentic. Individual orders, statements, everything. I'm going challenge all of that, even if I go on for 100 years, that cannot be admitted into evidence without leading proper evidence regarding authenticity. Of course you and your colleagues make the final judgement on the probative value and relevance of evidence. However, it is for me to challenge what they are saying and to fight the Prosecution. I will do that persistently. There are some basic facts. Those are texts of laws accessible to all and everything else it can also be excerpts from my books. I'm not going to challenge that; I'm very proud of my books. A lot of evidence pertains to that too. However, everything where authenticity is not proven I will persistently and bitterly challenge. If I receive alleged stenographic notes on the establishment of the Serbian Democratic Party and I never attended that meeting, that Assembly, the Prosecution has to prove that through a witness who's going to say, Yes, those authentic stenographic notes from that Assembly. Otherwise, it cannot be admitted into evidence. Well, it can be admitted but through violent means, violent methods. In many trials before this Tribunal these violent methods were applied. You know, I carefully studied Mr. Milosevic's case and that is why most of my examples have to do with that particular case, because the Serbian Radical Party, in 38 books and periodicals, published all the trial documents except for closed sessions. I learned a great deal from that trial. When Mr. Milosevic asked for a judgement of a Serbian court to be admitted into evidence, the Prosecution challenged that and the Trial Chamber ruled irrelevant, cannot be admitted, Serbian courts cannot be trusted. But even when the most meaningless statement of the other side in this war is proffered that is admitted. I'm going challenge that throughout, every inch of the way. Case-law and jurisprudence can be binding to a certain degree, but not negative case-law, especially not case-law which I can prove is negative. I will go on challenging that and disputing it. Secondly, the Prosecution wants a certain number of documents to be admitted into evidence along with statements and testimonies by dead witnesses from other trials. How could that be possible? That is beyond belief. That cannot be done in common law or in civil law. Nowhere. Of course, a document can be evidence in its own right. The Prosecution can, within their opening statements, proffer a certain number of documents, but those are the type of documents that are not contested by their nature, official documents published in Official Gazettes and, in this case, excerpts from my book. I'm just going to have a careful look to see whether they forged something at some -- in some place. So far they haven't falsified or forged anything, and I assume they won't do that in the future either. And that's it. They can also present video-clips of my speeches. I'm not going to challenge that either. Everything else I'm going challenge because it is my right to challenge. If I don't have time to challenge, then that will be a problem for the Trial Chamber. It won't be my problem. I have to have to the opportunity to challenge everything; otherwise, they will be compelled to make restrictions. You know, for them to make a list of exhibits that they did not have time to include along with the testimony of some witnesses and to ask to have this admitted automatically, that is impermissible to my mind. That is not allowed by common law or continental law. In continental law, the Prosecutor is not trusted a priori. In continental law, the Prosecutor is one of the parties. Not a single police report is admitted in continental law, not a single police note. Not a single hearing by the police, or interview, whereas they were cases here where this was directly admitted into evidence. Illegal wire-tapping evidence in continental law is never admitted into evidence, whereas there are cases here where illegal wire-taps were admitted into evidence. Illegal wire-taps -- wire-taps were admitted into evidence. Very rarely was the authenticity of these recordings questioned. In this case, the Prosecution offered many taped telephone conversations, most of them are highly irrelevant, in my view. But as for every one of these intercepts they will first and foremost have to submit proof as to how legal it was to wire-tap these phones. And a witness with only an elementary education, without any education cannot recognise my voice or the voice of my interlocutor. What kind of evidence is that? A expert has to ascertain how authentic my voice is in the case of an intercept. That is it something that cannot be challenged in law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will consider the matter. But here again, I may tell you what I think about the matter personally. You're talking about wire-tapping, and I don't know the case file, I don't know if your voice has been recorded, if there are any intercepts with your voice on it. But let's assume that your voice has been recorded, illegally or not, I'm not quite sure. If you have been recorded, the recording will be played at trial. You will be in a position to listen to it, and you may say, It's not my voice. The recording has been tampered with. According to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Trial Chamber may exclude any evidence when the probative value of the evidence does not comply with the principle of a fair trial. Therefore, any evidence may be dismissed. I have listened very carefully to you, and it seems to me that you are concerned, you are concerned because some things happened in another trial and you challenged the procedure in another trial. Rest assured, that the Trial Chamber in this case will examine and consider the matter conscientiously when it comes to admission of evidence. You mentioned the issue of authenticity. If you believe that a given document is not authentic because, according to you, it is a forgery, you will have the opportunity to say so. When it comes to the reliability of a document, a number of factors are taken into account. Let me give them to you for your information. When we are dealing with documents, especially military, state, public documents, police documents, usually you have a stamp on such documents. You have a signature, a date, a registration number, and then you have the document proper. If a document is challenged because of its authenticity, the Trial Chamber will review the document according to all the factors I have just listed. That's the way we go about it. If you believe that the stamp is a forgery, that the signature is not the signature of the person it pertains to be, you may say so and you may bring your evidence against this. Believe me, Mr. Seselj, there may be documents that have been fabricated, forged, but professional Judges will notice that immediately. It very rarely happens that an accused is prejudiced because a Trial Chamber has admitted the document without further adieu. Although a party to the proceedings, the Prosecution has to apply a number of ethical principles. The Prosecution may not provide any document without any checks. As part of the adversarial system, you will be in a position to challenge these documents, will have the opportunity to deal with this matter later. We now need to have a 20-minute break because the interpreters need a rest, and we need to change the tapes. 20-minute break, thus --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I'm being told that the interpreters working with us today have been working since this morning, and they can't work later than 6.00 p.m. Further more, we need to have a break for technical reasons. We need to change the tape. Therefore, I find myself in a position where I have not been able to deal with all the issues I wanted to deal with. We'll meet again as soon as practically possible to continue these Status Conferences in preparation for your trial. Let me tell you briefly what will be the next time we meet. I wanted to deal with the pending motions, but of course you're yourself familiar with these motions. I intended to deal with the matter of disclosure, but that's a matter that has been discussed at length already; and I also wanted to deal with the matter of the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination, but we have to stop for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm being told that we have five minutes left. Five minutes. Mr. Seselj, do you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not in respect of what we have been discussing so as far. I could discuss some new matters, but I can leave that for the next Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Dahl, do you have other topics you'd like to deal with within the very few minutes left to us?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Just a final word. Mr. Seselj, the detention conditions nothing to say. Health-wise, is that okay too?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The legal officer is telling me this yesterday very quickly, we dealt with the issue of your associate, the one who must meet the requirements as per Rule 45 of the Rules. Let me reassure you totally in saying this. In the part of the decision related to the implementation of Rule 45, the only condition is that one of the members of your team, including those in Belgrade and possibly those who will come to The Hague, that one of them only be a lawyer or be a professor of law. You've already told me that there were some who were lawyers or professors of law in your list. That means that the condition is met. As far as I can see, it cannot be required of those are to come to The Hague. It is enough for you to have among the group of people assisting you here or in Belgrade or elsewhere just one person who is either a lawyer or a professor of law. That's all I wanted to say. The time has come to conclude. Thank you. I thank all the participants for their very good behaviour. It's been quite a long day. It was long on Friday already, and I look forward to meeting you soon. The hearing stands adjourned.
